title: Clocks, ordering, logical and hybrid clocks, clock skew
scopeHtml:
Scope: Wall vs monotonic clocks, NTP skew, happened-before, Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks, TrueTime, sequencers.

Scope: Wall vs monotonic clocks, NTP skew, happened-before, Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks, TrueTime, sequencers.

notes.title: Why time is hard in distributed systems
notes.html:
Two machines never agree exactly on what time it is, and no message arrives instantly. So you cannot answer "which of these two events happened first?" by comparing wall-clock timestamps from different machines.

Each computer has a quartz crystal that drifts. Typical drift is about 10 to 100 parts per million, i.e. 1 to 9 seconds per day if never corrected. NTP corrects it over the network, but the accuracy depends on network delay: roughly 1 to 10 ms in a good datacenter, tens of ms over the internet.

Worked example. Server B's clock is 45 ms ahead. B writes balance=50 at real time 12:00:00.000, stamping it 12:00:00.045. Then A (correct clock) writes balance=100 20 ms later, at real time 12:00:00.020, stamped 12:00:00.020. A's write is really newer, but B's timestamp (.045) is larger, so "last write wins by timestamp" keeps B's 50 and silently discards A's 100.

Industry examples. Cassandra uses last-write-wins by client or coordinator timestamp, and its docs warn about clock skew losing writes. Google built Spanner with special hardware (GPS and atomic clocks) precisely because ordinary clocks are not trustworthy enough.

Everyday analogy. Ten people each wearing a watch that is a few minutes off, all trying to agree who arrived at a party first by comparing watches. They cannot; they need another way to order arrivals.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "just use timestamps" for ordering across machines.
  • Confusing wall-clock time (can jump backwards) with monotonic time (only moves forward, but is only meaningful on one machine).
  • Assuming NTP makes clocks equal. It makes them close, not equal.

notes.title: Wall clock vs monotonic clock
notes.html:
A wall clock tells the date and time and can be adjusted; a monotonic clock only counts elapsed time and never goes backwards.

  • Wall clock: System.currentTimeMillis() in Java/Kotlin, time.time() in Python. NTP can step it forward or backward, and leap seconds or an admin can change it.
  • Monotonic clock: System.nanoTime(), SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() on Android, time.monotonic(). Perfect for measuring durations and timeouts on ONE machine. The absolute value is meaningless and not comparable across machines.
// Wrong: wall clock can jump back (NTP step) and give a negative or huge duration
val start = System.currentTimeMillis()
doWork()
val elapsed = System.currentTimeMillis() - start

// Right: monotonic for durations and timeouts
val t0 = System.nanoTime()
doWork()
val elapsedMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000

Real incident pattern. A lease or cache TTL computed from wall clock; NTP steps the clock back 30 s; entries live 30 s too long or a lock holder believes it still holds a lease. Metric that shows it: negative durations or TTL anomalies right after an NTP step log line.

Industry examples. Cloudflare had an outage in 2017 caused by a negative number from time subtraction around a leap second (a Go time.Now() difference went negative; Go later added monotonic readings to time.Time). Java's Instant.now() is wall clock; use nanoTime for timers.

Decision gravity. Using the right clock type is a free, reversible choice in code, but bugs hide for months until the first clock step. Always default to monotonic for timeouts.

Everyday analogy. A wall clock is the clock on the wall that someone can reset after a power cut; a monotonic clock is a stopwatch: it can only tell how long, not what time.

Common interview traps.

  • Using currentTimeMillis for timeouts, rate limiters or benchmarks.
  • Comparing nanoTime values from two different JVMs or machines.

notes.title: Clock skew, drift and NTP
notes.html:
Drift is a clock running at the wrong speed; skew is the difference between two clocks at one instant. NTP reduces skew by periodically asking time servers and adjusting.

How NTP gets the offset: the client sends request at T1, server receives at T2, replies at T3, client receives at T4. Offset is estimated as ((T2 - T1) + (T3 - T4)) / 2, assuming the network path is symmetric. Asymmetric delays give error up to half the round trip.

Two ways to fix a clock:

  • Step: jump to the right time. Dangerous (time may go backwards).
  • Slew: run slightly faster or slower (e.g. up to 500 ppm in Linux adjtime style) until corrected. Safer. chrony and ntpd slew small errors and step only big ones.

Worked example. Round trip is 20 ms. Offset error can be up to +-10 ms even when everything works. Over a bad link with 200 ms round trip, +-100 ms. A skew of 100 ms is enough to reorder two writes made 50 ms apart.

Leap seconds. A leap second adds a repeated 23:59:59. Google and AWS "smear" it, spreading the extra second over many hours, so clocks never see a repeated second. Servers that mix smeared and non-smeared time sources disagree by up to 0.5 s.

Industry examples. AWS Time Sync Service and Google's public NTP both offer smeared time. Cloud providers advertise sub-millisecond sync on newer instances with PTP hardware clocks (confirm exact numbers in the current docs).

Everyday analogy. Several friends correct their watches by phoning the speaking clock; the line delay means each ends up a bit off, and a few jump their watch while others quietly speed it up.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing that two NTP-synced servers are within microseconds.
  • Not knowing that a backward step breaks lease and timeout logic.
  • Mixing leap-smear and non-smear NTP pools in one fleet.

notes.title: Happened-before and causality
notes.html:
Event A happened-before event B (A -> B) if A could have caused B. Lamport defined it by three rules: (1) events on the same process are ordered by their order in that process; (2) sending a message happens before receiving it; (3) it is transitive. If neither A -> B nor B -> A, the events are concurrent: no information could have flowed between them.

This is the right notion of order for distributed systems: not "what time was it" but "could one have influenced the other".

Worked example. Alice posts "I got the job" (event a). Bob sees it and comments "Congrats!" (event b). a -> b because Bob's comment was caused by seeing the post. If a replica shows the comment without the post, causality is violated. That is a causal consistency bug, not a clock bug.

Industry examples. Facebook TAO and Cassandra-like stores track causality for comment/reply ordering; MongoDB has causal-consistency sessions using cluster time; COPS and Riak research systems popularized causal+ consistency.

Decision gravity. Choosing causal ordering over total ordering is a design decision: cheaper (no global coordination) but gives only a partial order. Total order needs consensus (see Raft). Mostly reversible at the API level only if clients do not rely on the stronger guarantee.

Everyday analogy. A reply in a WhatsApp group: you can only reply after you saw the message. Two people typing at the same moment without seeing each other are concurrent.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating "concurrent" as "same time". It means unordered by causality.
  • Saying causality needs synchronized clocks. It does not.

notes.title: Lamport logical clocks
notes.html:
A Lamport clock is a single counter per process that gives every event a number consistent with happened-before.

Rules:

  1. Before each local event, L = L + 1.
  2. When sending, attach L to the message.
  3. On receiving a message with timestamp Lm, set L = max(L, Lm) + 1.

Guarantee: if A -> B then L(A) < L(B). The reverse is NOT true: L(A) < L(B) does not mean A caused B. A Lamport timestamp cannot detect concurrency.

Tie-break equal numbers by process ID to get a total order consistent with causality.

class Lamport:
    def __init__(self):
        self.t = 0
    def tick(self):          # local event or send
        self.t += 1
        return self.t
    def receive(self, tm):   # on message
        self.t = max(self.t, tm) + 1
        return self.t

Worked example. P1: event a (L=1), sends to P2 with 1. P2 has L=5 locally, receives: max(5,1)+1 = 6. P3 independently does an event with L=2. Order by (L, id): a(1), c(2), receive(6). Totally ordered, but c and a were concurrent; the order is an arbitrary but consistent choice.

Industry examples. Lamport timestamps are used to order operations in replicated state machines and mutual exclusion algorithms; Kafka-like offsets and database LSNs are the same idea of a monotonic sequence assigned by one authority.

Everyday analogy. Take-a-number tickets at a bank where, when you talk to someone with a higher number, you bump yours above it.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming L(A) < L(B) implies A happened-before B.
  • Forgetting the +1 after the max on receive.

notes.title: Vector clocks and version vectors
notes.html:
A vector clock keeps one counter per process, so it CAN tell causal order from concurrency.

Each process i keeps a vector V of size N. Rules: on a local event V[i]++; on send attach V; on receive, take the element-wise max with the message vector, then V[i]++.

Compare two vectors: A <= B if every element of A is <= B. If A <= B and A != B then A happened-before B. If neither A <= B nor B <= A, they are concurrent: a conflict that needs resolving.

3 nodes, vectors [n1, n2, n3]
n1 writes x:      [1,0,0]
n2 reads, writes: [1,1,0]    (after seeing [1,0,0])  -> causally after
n3 writes x:      [0,0,1]    (never saw n1/n2)
[1,1,0] vs [0,0,1]: neither <= the other  => CONCURRENT => conflict, keep both siblings

Version vectors are the same idea but track versions of a data item per replica rather than events.

Cost. Vector size grows with the number of writers. Dynamo-style systems truncate or prune old entries (risking false conflicts), and Riak moved to dotted version vectors to keep size bounded and avoid sibling explosions.

Industry examples. Amazon's Dynamo paper used vector clocks and returned siblings to the client to merge (the shopping cart). Riak used them and later dotted version vectors. Cassandra deliberately chose timestamps (LWW) instead for simplicity, accepting lost updates.

Decision gravity. Vector clocks vs LWW: vectors detect conflicts and lose no data but push merge logic to the app (hard); LWW is simple but silently drops writes. Switching later changes the data model, so it is nearly a one-way door.

Everyday analogy. Each friend keeps a notebook of "how many messages I have seen from each person". Comparing notebooks tells you who is ahead or whether you each saw different things.

Common interview traps.

  • Not knowing the cost: O(N) per timestamp.
  • Saying vector clocks resolve conflicts. They detect them; the application merges (or you use CRDTs).

notes.title: Hybrid logical clocks
notes.html:
A hybrid logical clock (HLC) packs physical time and a logical counter into one value that stays close to real time AND respects causality.

An HLC timestamp is (l, c): l is the largest physical time the node has seen, c is a counter for events with the same l. Rules (simplified): on a local/send event, l' = max(l, pt); if l' == l then c++ else c = 0. On receive, l' = max(l, lm, pt) and the counter is bumped accordingly. Timestamps fit in 64 bits (e.g. 48 bits of ms plus 16 bits of counter), unlike vector clocks.

Properties: monotonic per node, causality preserved (if A -> B then HLC(A) < HLC(B)), and l never drifts more than the max clock skew from true time, so humans can read it ("about 14:03:07").

Worked example. Node A physical time is 100 ms, B's is 90 ms (10 ms behind). A sends message with (100,0). B's physical 90 is behind, so on receive B sets l = max(90, 100) = 100, c = 1, giving (100,1). B's next event is (100,2) even though its wall clock still says 91. Causality holds despite skew.

Industry examples. CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use HLC for MVCC timestamps (CockroachDB also enforces a max clock offset, default 500 ms, and nodes that exceed it terminate themselves; confirm in docs for your version). MongoDB's cluster time is HLC-like.

Decision gravity. HLC is the pragmatic middle: fixed 8-byte size, human-readable, no special hardware. It cannot detect concurrency like vector clocks, and if skew exceeds the configured bound correctness can degrade. Reversible only with a data migration of stored timestamps.

Everyday analogy. A diary with the date at the top and a "#n of the day" for entries on the same day; if a friend tells you their diary is already on a later date, you jump forward to that date.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming HLC gives external consistency. That needs bounded uncertainty like TrueTime.
  • Forgetting the max-offset assumption.

notes.title: TrueTime and bounded uncertainty
notes.html:
TrueTime returns a time interval [earliest, latest] instead of one number, and the real time is guaranteed to be inside it. Google Spanner uses GPS receivers and atomic clocks in each datacenter; the published uncertainty is typically a few ms (about 1 to 7 ms in the paper; confirm current numbers).

Commit wait. Spanner assigns a commit timestamp s, then waits until TT.now().earliest > s before making the commit visible. That wait (about the uncertainty, a few ms) guarantees any transaction that starts later sees a larger timestamp, giving external consistency (linearizability across the planet).

Worked example. Uncertainty 7 ms, so each read-write commit adds up to about 7 ms latency. At 1,000 commits/s per group that wait overlaps (it is per transaction, not serialized), so throughput is not capped, only latency grows.

Industry examples. Google Spanner. AWS offers Time Sync with tight bounds, and Amazon Aurora DSQL and others use similar clock-bound ideas (confirm per service). CockroachDB approximates it with uncertainty intervals and restarts of reads.

Decision gravity. Buying precise clocks (hardware, ops) is a one-way infrastructure door; it simplifies the application contract (strong consistency) but ties you to a provider. Alternative: logical clocks and a timestamp oracle (TiDB's PD, Percolator style): a single service hands out increasing numbers, simple but a bottleneck and a cross-region latency cost.

Everyday analogy. Saying "it is between 12:00:00 and 12:00:07" and then waiting 7 seconds before announcing the winner so nobody can claim they finished first.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking TrueTime removes the need for waiting. The wait is what buys correctness.
  • Saying any system with NTP can do external consistency.

notes.title: Ordering with a single authority: sequences and oracles
notes.html:
The simplest way to order events is to let ONE component number them. Databases use a WAL position (LSN), Kafka uses a per-partition offset, Twitter used Snowflake IDs, TiDB uses a timestamp oracle.

Snowflake IDs (Twitter's design): 64 bits = 41 bits of ms timestamp (about 69 years) + 10 bits machine ID (1,024 workers) + 12 bits sequence (4,096 IDs per ms per worker). IDs are roughly time-ordered and generated without coordination. Danger: if the wall clock moves backwards the generator must refuse or wait, otherwise IDs collide; this is a classic clock-skew bug.

Worked example. Kafka partition guarantees order only inside one partition. 10 partitions give no global order; to order all events for a user, key by user ID so they land in the same partition.

Industry examples. Instagram (Postgres-based ID with timestamp + shard + sequence), Discord (Snowflake variant), MongoDB ObjectId (timestamp + machine + counter).

Decision gravity. Single authority per partition: simple and fast, but the authority is a bottleneck/failure point (hence leader election, see consensus notes). Global total order needs a single sequencer or consensus. Changing the ordering scheme means re-keying data: close to a one-way door.

Everyday analogy. The deli ticket dispenser: one machine means no arguments about who is next.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting a global order across Kafka partitions.
  • Ignoring clock-going-backwards handling in Snowflake generators.

notes.title: Choosing a clock strategy in an interview
notes.html:
Pick the cheapest tool that satisfies the requirement:

Need Use
Timeouts, rate limits on one machine Monotonic clock
Roughly sort log lines, debugging Wall-clock timestamps plus a trace ID
Causal order of messages, no concurrency detection Lamport clock
Detect conflicting concurrent updates Vector / version vectors, or CRDTs
Order transactions, readable, no special hardware HLC
Global external consistency TrueTime-style bounded clocks or one timestamp oracle
Unique sortable IDs Snowflake-style IDs

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing vector clocks for a million clients (vector size explodes).
  • Reaching for Spanner-level machinery when a leader with a counter is enough.
  • Not stating the failure assumption (max skew, message delay).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Wall clocks drift (10-100 ppm) and skew; NTP gives roughly ms accuracy, never equality. Do not order cross-machine events by wall-clock time.
  • Use monotonic clocks for durations and timeouts; wall clocks can jump back.
  • Happened-before defines causal order; events with no causal path are concurrent.
  • Lamport: one counter, max+1, respects causality but cannot detect concurrency. Vector clocks: O(N) size, detect concurrency, conflicts need merging (Dynamo, Riak).
  • HLC: 64-bit physical+logical, causal, human-readable (CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, MongoDB). TrueTime: bounded uncertainty plus commit wait gives external consistency (Spanner).
  • Often the best answer is a single sequencer per partition (LSN, Kafka offset, Snowflake) rather than clever clocks.
  • LWW by timestamp silently loses writes under skew; know that trade-off.

questions.subtopic: Why wall clocks cannot order events
questions.promptHtml: Two services on different machines both stamp their writes with now(). Why can't I just sort by those timestamps to know which write came first?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common junior mistake in distributed design is trusting timestamps across machines. They want to see you know why and what replaces them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every machine's clock drifts and is only corrected approximately by NTP, so two clocks can disagree by milliseconds to hundreds of milliseconds. If two writes are closer together than that error, the timestamp order can be the opposite of the real order. For ordering across machines I use causal order (logical clocks), a single sequencer, or clocks with a bounded error, not raw wall-clock time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• A quartz crystal drifts about 10 to 100 ppm, which is 1 to 9 seconds a day uncorrected. NTP corrects it, but accuracy depends on network delay: about 1 to 10 ms in a datacenter, tens of ms over the internet.
  • Skew example: B is 45 ms ahead. B writes balance=50 at real time 0 (stamped .045). A writes balance=100 at real time +20 ms (stamped .020). Last-write-wins by timestamp keeps B's value, discarding the newer write.
  • The question "which came first" is really "could one have influenced the other"; that is happened-before, and it needs no synchronized clocks.
real time:   0ms           20ms
B (+45ms):   write 50 @45
A (exact):                 write 100 @20
LWW by stamp: 45 > 20  => keeps 50  (WRONG, 100 was newer)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "NTP makes clocks equal". It makes them close, not equal.
  • Using last-write-wins and not realizing it silently drops data.
  • Confusing this with wall vs monotonic clocks (a different problem on one machine).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What do I use instead? -> Lamport/vector clocks for causality, HLC for readable causal timestamps, a per-partition sequencer, or TrueTime-style bounded clocks.
  2. Is wall time ever fine across machines? -> Yes for human-readable logs and rough sorting, ideally with a trace ID.
  3. Which real database accepts this risk? -> Cassandra uses timestamp LWW and documents clock-skew write loss.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "use NTP". The senior answer quantifies the skew (ms), names the failure (silent lost write), and picks a mechanism by requirement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: LWW stores lose acknowledged writes when one node's clock runs ahead; the symptom is "my update vanished" with no error anywhere.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a wall clock and a monotonic clock, and which one do I use to measure a timeout?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Quick filter for engineers who have debugged real timeout and lease bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A wall clock tells the date and time and can jump forwards or backwards when NTP steps it or an admin changes it. A monotonic clock only counts elapsed time and never goes back, but its absolute value means nothing and cannot be compared across machines. I use monotonic for durations, timeouts and rate limits, wall clock only when I need a calendar time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Java/Kotlin: System.currentTimeMillis() and Instant.now() are wall clock; System.nanoTime() is monotonic. Python: time.time() vs time.monotonic(). Android: SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() is monotonic.
  • A backward step of 30 s makes now - start negative or lets a lease live 30 s too long.
  • Monotonic values are per-process/per-boot; storing a nanoTime in a DB or sending it to another machine is meaningless.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
long t0 = System.nanoTime();
doWork();
long elapsedMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000;
val t0 = System.nanoTime()
doWork()
val elapsedMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Timeouts, rate limiters or benchmarks built on currentTimeMillis.
  • Comparing nanoTime from two JVMs.
  • Assuming the bug will show up in tests; it appears at the first clock step in production.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a monotonic clock be wrong? -> It can still run slightly fast or slow (drift), but it never jumps back.
  2. How do you persist a deadline across restarts? -> Store a wall-clock deadline, and re-derive a monotonic remaining time on load.
  3. What did the 2017 Cloudflare leap-second outage teach? -> A negative duration from wall-clock subtraction broke code; Go later added monotonic readings to time.Time.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer defines both. The senior adds the failure mode (negative durations and over-long leases after an NTP step), the cross-machine caveat and the persistence caveat.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: TTL caches and lease logic built on wall clock misbehaved right after NTP step log lines; the clue is negative durations in metrics.

questions.contextHtml: A user-profile service runs on a Cassandra-like store with last-write-wins by coordinator timestamp, 6 nodes, about 3,000 writes/s. Support reports that about 20 users per day see their "display name" revert to an older value minutes after they changed it. The app has no error logs. Two clients (web and mobile) sometimes update the same profile within a few hundred ms of each other. Dashboards show CPU 30% and replication healthy. chronyc tracking on one node shows System time: 0.180 seconds fast of NTP time.
questions.promptHtml: Find the cause, say how you would confirm it and what you would change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Probably a race condition in the app; add a lock." It ignores that the store resolves conflicts by timestamp and never checks clocks.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which coordinator handled the losing write (skew is per node)? Does the revert correlate with a specific node? Are web and mobile writing the same column? Is the store using client or server timestamps?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the 180 ms offset first: restart chrony/step the node safely or drain it from coordinator duty.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) one node's clock 180 ms fast, so its writes always win LWW; (b) NTP unreachable on that host; (c) client-side timestamps with bad device clocks; (d) read-repair bug (red herring: replication looks healthy).
  4. How I'd verify each: chronyc tracking and chronyc sources on all nodes; compare write timestamps (WRITETIME(col)) of a reverted row with the coordinator that handled it; check server logs for the NTP daemon.
  5. Root cause: Writes coordinated by the fast node get a stamp 180 ms in the future. A later real write via a correct node, within 180 ms, carries a smaller timestamp and loses.
  6. Fix: Short term: repair NTP, alert on offset above, say, 50 ms. Long term: for fields where concurrent updates matter use conditional writes (lightweight transactions) or a version column, or move conflict detection to version vectors.
  7. Prevention: Monitor clock offset on every node (node_timex_offset_seconds in node_exporter), alert on it, keep a single time source policy.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add an application lock (it does not touch the store's timestamps) and would not move everything to LWT, which costs about 4 round trips per write.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the clocks were perfect? -> Two near-simultaneous writes still pick an arbitrary winner; LWW cannot detect concurrency, only vector clocks or CAS can.
  • Could client-supplied timestamps help? -> They move the skew to millions of uncontrolled device clocks; worse.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fleet had one VM whose NTP daemon was blocked by a firewall change. Its clock slowly ran 400 ms fast and a handful of "my change reverted" tickets took three weeks to connect to it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames app races or caching, never inspects clocks.
  • Hire: identifies skew and LWW, confirms with chronyc and WRITETIME, fixes NTP.
  • Strong hire: adds offset alerting, explains that concurrency cannot be detected by LWW at all, proposes CAS or version vectors where it matters.

questions.contextHtml:
A cache entry and a worker lease are implemented as below. Ops see that after a maintenance window where NTP stepped the clock back by 30 s, some cache entries lived about 30 s too long and one worker kept running a job after its lease should have expired. Lease is 20 s.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class Lease {
    private final long expiresAt;               // epoch millis
    Lease(long ttlMs) { this.expiresAt = System.currentTimeMillis() + ttlMs; }
    boolean isValid() { return System.currentTimeMillis() < expiresAt; }
}
class Lease(ttlMs: Long) {
    private val expiresAt = System.currentTimeMillis() + ttlMs   // epoch millis
    fun isValid() = System.currentTimeMillis() < expiresAt
}
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug, what exactly happened in the incident, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Time zones" or "add a buffer". It misses that a backward step stretches every deadline.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the lease also stored remotely (shared across hosts)? Is there a safety margin against drift? Does anything compare this deadline with another machine's clock?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart affected workers or invalidate caches after a known clock step.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: the wall clock was stepped back (NTP); a VM resume jumped time; manual date change.
  4. How I'd verify each: grep chrony/ntpd logs for "Time was stepped"/"System clock wrong by"; check journalctl -u chronyd; look for a dip in a wall-clock-based graph.
  5. Root cause: Deadline is an absolute wall-clock instant; if the clock moves back 30 s the deadline is 30 s further away in real time.
  6. Fix: Use a monotonic base: store System.nanoTime() at creation and compare differences. For a lease shared with other machines, the holder uses local monotonic time with a safety margin, and the resource enforces fencing (see locks notes).
  7. Prevention: Lint/code-review rule: no currentTimeMillis for timeouts; configure chrony to slew small errors (makestep only at boot).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not stop NTP to avoid steps; drift would then be worse. Monotonic time does not survive restart, so persistent deadlines still need a wall-clock value.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
class Lease {
    private final long startNs = System.nanoTime();
    private final long ttlNs;
    Lease(long ttlMs) { this.ttlNs = ttlMs * 1_000_000; }
    boolean isValid() { return System.nanoTime() - startNs < ttlNs; }
}
class Lease(ttlMs: Long) {
    private val startNs = System.nanoTime()
    private val ttlNs = ttlMs * 1_000_000
    fun isValid() = System.nanoTime() - startNs < ttlNs
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the VM is paused for 60 s? -> Monotonic clocks may or may not count suspended time depending on the OS (verify); either way the holder cannot know, so the resource must fence.
  • What about a forward step? -> Entries expire early; usually safe but can cause a thundering herd of refreshes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rate limiter using wall clock allowed a burst of 4x traffic for 30 s after a clock step, which was enough to trip a downstream circuit breaker.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot explain how a backward step lengthens the lease.
  • Hire: switches to monotonic and explains the incident.
  • Strong hire: also covers persistence, VM pauses, and fencing for shared leases.

questions.promptHtml: What can a vector clock tell me that a Lamport clock cannot, and what does it cost?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you really understand causality vs a mere total order.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Lamport timestamp guarantees that if A happened-before B then L(A) < L(B), but the reverse does not hold, so it cannot tell "A caused B" from "A and B were concurrent". A vector clock keeps one counter per node, so comparing two vectors says before, after or concurrent. The cost is O(N) size per timestamp, and detection only: the application still has to merge conflicts.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Lamport: one integer; local event L+1; on receive max(L, Lm)+1. Tie-break by node ID for a total order.
  • Vector: node i does V[i]++ locally, sends V, and on receive takes the element-wise max then V[i]++.
  • A <= B if every element is <=. If neither A <= B nor B <= A the events are concurrent.
n1 writes x: [1,0,0]
n2 after seeing it, writes: [1,1,0]   -> after [1,0,0]
n3 writes without seeing: [0,0,1]
[1,1,0] vs [0,0,1] -> neither <= -> CONCURRENT -> keep siblings
  • Size grows with writers; Dynamo-style stores prune (risking false conflicts) and Riak moved to dotted version vectors.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming L(A) < L(B) implies causality.
  • Saying vector clocks resolve conflicts; they only detect them.
  • Using per-client vectors for a million clients.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where would you use Lamport? -> When you only need a total order consistent with causality, e.g. replicated state machines or mutual exclusion.
  2. How do vector clocks relate to version vectors? -> Same idea, but counters track versions of one data item per replica rather than process events.
  3. How do you avoid manual merges? -> CRDTs, which make the merge function commutative and idempotent.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Junior: "vector clocks order events better". Senior: detects concurrency vs only ordering, O(N) cost, who merges, pruning pitfalls.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Dynamo-style cart services surface siblings and a bad merge resurrects deleted items; Cassandra chose LWW to avoid this complexity.

questions.contextHtml: Product says: "Messages in a chat must always show in the right order." The chat has 2M DAU, about 15,000 messages/s at peak, 1:1 and group conversations up to 500 members, multi-region (US, EU). The first design stamps each message with the sender's phone clock and sorts by it. Beta users see replies appear above the messages they reply to.
questions.promptHtml: How do you proceed? Assume the interviewer wants to see you handle the ambiguity.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use server timestamps." It does not ask what order means (global? per conversation? causal?) and ignores multi-region.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is order needed globally or per conversation? (Almost always per conversation.) Must a reply always follow the message it answers (causal) or just a stable order everyone agrees on? Do users see messages sent while offline? Is cross-region write latency acceptable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop sorting by device time; sort by a server-assigned value.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) per-conversation sequence number from one authority (conversation hashed to a partition leader); (b) HLC for cross-region readable stamps; (c) vector clocks (overkill for this); (d) global sequencer (bottleneck).
  4. How I'd verify each: Estimate per-partition rate: 15,000/s over, say, 256 partitions is about 60/s each, trivial for one leader. Prove a reply carries the parent's sequence/id.
  5. Root cause: Device clocks are arbitrary, so order is arbitrary.
  6. Fix: Route each conversation to one partition/leader (Kafka-style key by conversation ID), assign a monotonically increasing seq, store it; the client shows by seq. Offline sends get a seq on arrival; a reply references parent_seq so the client can ensure it appears after.
  7. Prevention: Test with injected skew; property test that replies always follow parents.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The leader is a failure point per conversation, hence leader failover with epochs. I would not build a global total order; it costs a cross-region round trip for no user benefit. One-way door: the ordering scheme is baked into stored keys.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• User in EU chats with a friend in the US? -> Conversation home region owns the sequence; the remote user pays one cross-region RTT per send.
  • Leader fails mid-send? -> New leader continues with a higher epoch; clients retry with an idempotency key.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team added vector clocks to a chat for "correctness" and found payloads ballooning with group size; a per-conversation counter would have solved the actual requirement.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: server timestamps globally, no questions.
  • Hire: per-conversation sequencer and partitioning.
  • Strong hire: causal parent reference, failover with epochs, rejects global order with reasoning.

questions.contextHtml: You own a shopping-cart service on a Dynamo-style store, 3 replicas, 40,000 carts updated per minute at peak. Customers on phone and laptop sometimes edit the same cart within seconds while a network blip separates two replicas. Option A: last-write-wins by timestamp (current). Option B: vector clocks that return siblings, with the app merging by union of items. Complaints: "I removed an item and it came back" and "my new item vanished".
questions.promptHtml: Which do you choose and why? State the decision gravity.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Vector clocks are more correct, use them." It ignores the merge burden, deleted-item resurrection and the cost of switching.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is losing an add worse than resurrecting a removed item? How often are true concurrent edits (measure sibling rate)? How many writers per cart (bounded: a few devices)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep LWW but measure the lost-update rate (log when a write is overwritten within a 1 s window).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: the vanished item is LWW dropping a concurrent add; the resurrected item is a stale replica winning, or a union merge that cannot see deletes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay a sample of conflicts offline with both strategies; count differences.
  5. Root cause: LWW cannot detect concurrency; union merge treats a delete as absence of information.
  6. Fix: B, with an add-wins structure: carts are an observed-remove set (a CRDT-style design) with tombstones, so merge is deterministic and needs no user prompt. Writers per cart are few, so vector size stays small.
  7. Prevention: Cap sibling count, alert on sibling explosion, test merges with property-based tests (commutative, idempotent).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Costs: app complexity, tombstone growth, bigger values. This is nearly a one-way door because stored data and client contracts change; I would pilot on a shadow copy first. I would not use per-client vectors for all users.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Vector grows to 50 entries? -> Prune or use dotted version vectors; accept possible false conflicts.
  • Why not just lock the cart? -> Locks cost availability across the partition, which is why this store chose AP.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team shipped a "union merge" for carts and then received tickets about deleted coupons reappearing; tombstones with causal context fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks one without trade-offs.
  • Hire: explains detection vs resolution and picks vectors with a merge strategy.
  • Strong hire: discusses tombstones, CRDT-style merge, size bounds, migration risk.

questions.promptHtml: Explain a hybrid logical clock. Does it give external consistency like Spanner's TrueTime? Why or why not?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who memorized "CockroachDB uses HLC" from those who know what the guarantee is.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An HLC timestamp is (l, c): l is the max physical time this node has seen and c is a counter for events with the same l. It fits in 64 bits, tracks real time within the clock skew, and respects causality: if A happened-before B then HLC(A) < HLC(B). It does not give external consistency, because there is no bounded uncertainty and no commit wait; two non-causally-related transactions can be ordered differently from real time. TrueTime gets that by exposing an interval and waiting it out.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Local or send: l' = max(l, pt); if l' == l then c++ else c = 0. Receive: l' = max(l, lm, pt) with the counter bumped accordingly.
  • Example: A at 100 ms sends (100,0). B's physical clock says 90; on receive B sets (100,1), and its next event is (100,2) although its wall clock reads 91.
  • Guarantees: monotonic per node, causal, l within max skew of true time. Not guaranteed: detection of concurrency (unlike vectors), real-time ordering across unrelated clients.
  • Real-time ordering needs bounded uncertainty: TrueTime picks timestamp s then waits until TT.now().earliest > s (about a few ms).
  • CockroachDB uses HLC and a max-offset assumption (default 500 ms, verify per version), restarting reads that fall in an uncertainty window.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming HLC gives linearizability across the globe.
  • Forgetting the max-offset assumption; beyond it correctness can degrade.
  • Saying HLC detects concurrent writes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens if one clock is 2 s fast? -> Its l leaps ahead and pulls others forward via messages; physical time and l drift apart and the bound is violated, so systems kill offending nodes.
  2. Why include a counter? -> Many events can occur in one millisecond and need distinct, ordered stamps.
  3. How does CockroachDB still get strong behavior? -> Uncertainty intervals plus read restarts, giving single-key linearizability but not Spanner-style external consistency across unrelated transactions (verify the exact claims in docs).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "physical plus logical". The senior states exactly which property is kept and which is lost, and why commit wait buys the difference.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A database that self-terminated nodes at the clock offset bound turned a slow NTP change into a cluster-wide outage (see Q011).

questions.contextHtml: Order IDs come from a Snowflake-style generator: 41 bits ms timestamp, 10 bits worker ID, 12 bits sequence. After an NTP step the clock on worker 17 jumped back 2.3 s. For the next 2.3 s, about 600 orders/s were created. Afterwards the DB shows duplicate key value violates unique constraint "orders_pkey" errors and a few orders were silently attached to the wrong customer because an upsert-by-ID path was used. The generator code is ts = now(); if ts == last { seq = (seq+1) & 4095 } else { seq = 0 }; last = ts.
questions.promptHtml: Explain why IDs collided, how many, and what you change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the sequence bits." That does nothing for time moving backwards.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which write path used upsert (should have been insert)? Are IDs assigned before or after the DB call? How many workers share an ID?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Take worker 17 out of rotation, fix upsert paths to plain insert so a collision errors instead of overwriting, and list affected orders for manual repair.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: clock regression reuses (ms, worker, seq) tuples; two workers configured with the same worker ID (red herring: the errors are only on worker 17); sequence overflow (4,096 per ms is far above 600/s).
  4. How I'd verify each: SELECT id, count(*) on the ID prefix for worker 17 in the window; chrony logs for the step; compare worker ID registry.
  5. Root cause: After the regression the ms value repeats times already used 2.3 s earlier; the sequence restarts at 0 for each new ms, so tuples repeat. At 600/s that is roughly 600 x 2.3 = about 1,400 IDs potentially colliding with earlier ones (each reused ms had at least seq 0 before).
  6. Fix: Track last as max seen; if now < last either refuse and retry after waiting last - now (for small regression) or fail the node health check; never go below last. Use monotonic time to measure elapsed since startup and add to a base time. Make worker IDs unique via a lease in etcd/ZooKeeper.
  7. Prevention: Alert on clock offset and steps; make inserts non-upserting; unit test with a fake clock that goes backwards.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Waiting blocks ID creation for the regression length; refusing may be better for a large step. I would not "just continue with the old last timestamp" for hours.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Regression of 5 minutes? -> Fail the worker out; blocking 5 min is worse than failing over.
  • Could a DB sequence replace this? -> Yes, with a single-writer bottleneck and cross-region latency; Snowflake exists to avoid that.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A generator restart after a VM snapshot restore reused a worker ID plus an old timestamp range and produced duplicate IDs only visible weeks later in reconciliation.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames sequence bits or DB.
  • Hire: explains tuple reuse and fixes with max(last, now) plus wait/refuse.
  • Strong hire: quantifies collisions, worker ID uniqueness, upsert hazard, fake-clock test.

questions.contextHtml: You are designing a globally distributed ledger database: 3 regions (US-East, EU, AP), 5,000 read-write commits/s, p50 commit budget 60 ms, requirement "if transaction T1 commits before T2 starts, T2 must see T1" (external consistency). Option A: bounded-uncertainty clocks (GPS/atomic or cloud time sync with a published bound, assume uncertainty 7 ms) with commit wait. Option B: a single timestamp oracle in US-East handing out increasing timestamps; EU and AP are about 80 ms and 150 ms RTT from it (illustrative).
questions.promptHtml: Compare the two on latency, throughput, failure and decision gravity. Which do you pick?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "TrueTime is better because Google uses it." No numbers, no failure analysis.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can we get hardware or a cloud time service with a bound we trust? Are most transactions single-region? What is the read mix (reads can use snapshot timestamps)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design); I would prototype both on one workload.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: A adds commit wait of about the uncertainty (about 7 ms) per read-write commit, overlapped across transactions, so throughput is not capped. B adds at least one oracle RTT per transaction: 80 ms from EU, 150 ms from AP, already above the 60 ms budget for AP.
  4. How I'd verify each: Benchmark commit latency p50/p99; test oracle failover time; inject clock error beyond the bound and see how the system reacts.
  5. Root cause of the differences: A turns synchronization into waiting; B turns it into a message. Distance dominates B; hardware quality dominates A.
  6. Fix / decision: If the bound is trustworthy, A. B can batch timestamp requests and place a local oracle proxy per region, but cannot remove the cross-region RTT.
  7. Prevention: Monitor uncertainty; if it grows, commits slow down (graceful) rather than becoming incorrect.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A is a one-way infrastructure door and ties me to a provider; B is simple, but the oracle is a bottleneck and single point needing consensus. I would not claim external consistency on plain NTP.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Uncertainty rises to 50 ms during a time-sync outage? -> Commit wait grows to match; latency degrades but correctness holds; that is the design.
  • Could HLC substitute? -> It gives causal order but not real-time order for unrelated transactions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team picked a central oracle for a multi-region system and found AP writers stuck above 150 ms; they regionalized and gave up cross-region external consistency by product decision.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks by brand.
  • Hire: computes commit wait vs RTT and picks with reasons.
  • Strong hire: addresses uncertainty growth, failure behavior, vendor lock-in, and read-only snapshot reads.

questions.subtopic: NTP, leap smear and HLC offset
questions.contextHtml: A 9-node HLC-based SQL database (max clock offset configured at 500 ms) loses 3 nodes in 10 minutes, each exiting with clock synchronization error: this node is more than 500ms away from at least half of the known nodes. Nodes 1-6 sync to the cloud provider's NTP (leap-smearing) and nodes 7-9 were recently added from an image configured with pool.ntp.org (no smear). A leap second is being smeared over the next 24 hours. chronyc tracking on node 8 shows Last offset: -0.31 s and growing.
questions.promptHtml: Why are nodes dying, what do you do right now, and how do you prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart the nodes." They will crash again once offset passes the bound.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which nodes are crashing and which NTP source does each use? When does the smear end? How many nodes can fail before quorum is lost (9 nodes, tolerate 4)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop adding crashes: point nodes 7-9 at the same smearing source immediately (slewing, not stepping, to avoid a backward jump), and keep at most 4 nodes down. Consider temporarily raising max-offset only if the database docs allow it and the risk is understood.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: mixed smear/no-smear sources (offset up to about 0.5 s between them, matching the bound); bad NTP source; VM pause. Red herring: network latency looks normal.
  4. How I'd verify each: chronyc sources -v, chronyc tracking on every node, compare offsets; check the DB's own clock-offset metric (verify its name for your version).
  5. Root cause: Smeared nodes slowly shift up to about 0.5 s relative to an unsmeared reference during the smear window; once the divergence nears the max offset, the database kills nodes rather than risk wrong ordering.
  6. Fix: One time-source policy for the whole fleet (all smeared or all not), re-point 7-9 via config management, restart nodes one at a time.
  7. Prevention: Alert at 50% of max offset; image baselines enforce the chrony config; leap-second runbook.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not raise max-offset to hide it (weakens correctness) and would not step clocks backwards under live traffic.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does the database kill itself? -> Continuing with unbounded skew could violate its consistency guarantees; failing stop is safer than wrong data.
  • Is stopping NTP a fix? -> No; free-running drift reaches the bound within hours or days depending on ppm.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A new rack was provisioned from an old image with a different NTP pool; it passed health checks and caused two nodes to crash only during the leap event months later.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts, blames the database.
  • Hire: finds mixed smear sources and aligns NTP.
  • Strong hire: protects quorum while fixing, slews instead of steps, adds offset alerts and a leap-second runbook.

questions.contextHtml: A metadata service stores 800M records with writer-supplied wall-clock timestamps (LWW). Lost updates under skew are a recurring incident. You must move to HLC timestamps with no downtime. 60 app servers write at about 25,000 writes/s. Old readers/writers (some mobile clients on old app versions, up to 3 months old) still send wall-clock millis. The column is an int64 of epoch millis.
questions.promptHtml: Design the migration and name the risks.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run a script to rewrite all timestamps." It ignores compatibility and in-flight writers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a clean place to run the HLC (server side, not mobile)? Can the HLC be encoded in the same 64 bits (48 bits ms + 16 bits counter)? Are old clients allowed to supply timestamps?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ignore client timestamps: assign the version on the server so old clients no longer matter.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: encoding in place is risky because old values (pure ms) would compare below new (ms<<16) values; hence a version-number scheme change is needed.
  4. How I'd verify each: Dry-run comparison on a copy: do old values sort correctly relative to new? Shadow-write HLC next to the old timestamp and diff the winner decisions.
  5. Root cause of the risk: Mixing two encodings in one ordered column; ms vs ms<<16 differ by 65,536x, so old values would look ancient.
  6. Fix (plan): (1) add column hlc and dual-write both server-assigned; (2) backfill hlc = ms<<16 for old rows in batches, throttled; (3) switch conflict resolution to hlc; (4) deprecate client timestamps; (5) drop the old column after a bake period. Keep a feature flag per step.
  7. Prevention: Metric for "resolved by hlc != resolved by old ts" during shadow; enforce a max-offset guard rejecting HLC updates too far ahead of local time.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dual-write doubles write amplification for weeks; a one-shot rewrite at 800M rows would lock or saturate the store. HLC adds the max-offset dependency: a node with a clock far ahead can poison l for everyone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A bad node pushes l one hour ahead? -> Reject messages exceeding the allowed offset and alert; otherwise all HLCs jump.
  • Rollback? -> Possible until step 3; after that old column is stale, so keep dual-write until confidence.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration that reinterpreted an existing column in place left old rows sorting before everything; a shadow column and a flag turned a risky big-bang into a dull rollout.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one-shot rewrite.
  • Hire: phased dual-write and backfill.
  • Strong hire: addresses encoding mismatch, old clients, offset guard, rollback and write amplification.
